analysis.one_liner: Ends tax-favored retirement contributions for high earners whose accounts already top $10 million.
analysis.headline: A senior House Democrat introduced the bill in July 2026 with zero cosponsors; the Ways and Means Committee has taken no action beyond the initial referral, and no vote has occurred.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets a narrow group: taxpayers earning above roughly $400,000 (or $450,000 for married couples) who have more than $10 million stacked up across their retirement accounts. It bars them from making any new tax-preferred retirement contributions once balances pass that $10 million line, and starting in 2034 it forces them to draw down at least half of the excess each year, including from tax-free Roth accounts. Everyone with balances below $10 million is untouched, and rollovers, inheritances, and divorce transfers don't count against the limit.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, ordinary taxpayers would get a slightly larger tax base and a fairness fix: the richest account holders could no longer keep stuffing tens of millions into shelters designed for ordinary retirement saving. People who felt the tax code lets the largest balances compound tax-free while their own savings get taxed would see the most extreme cases trimmed.

how_it_helps.text: For taxpayers with incomes above the thresholds (about $400,000 single, $450,000 married), the bill prohibits new contributions to IRAs and workplace retirement plans once their total vested balances exceed $10 million.

Starting in 2034, affected taxpayers must take minimum distributions equal to at least half the excess over $10 million each year, shrinking balances that otherwise grow tax-free or tax-deferred indefinitely.
The income thresholds and the $10 million balance line adjust for inflation after 2027, so the limits keep pace with prices.

analysis.who_pays: A very small group of high-income taxpayers with retirement balances above $10 million, who would be barred from contributing further and forced to sell investments to make the required drawdowns. Wealth managers handling those mega-accounts would see assets move out.

drawbacks.text: Most of the forced drawdown can be taken from Roth IRAs and Roth accounts, which the bill treats as tax-free qualified distributions, so it raises little new revenue and mainly forces portfolio sales rather than collecting taxes [S2].

The bill carves out employee stock ownership plan shares that are not readily tradable on an established market, shielding owners of closely held businesses from the accelerated drawdown while ordinary liquid accounts are hit [S2].
The $10 million threshold leaves the first $10 million of tax-advantaged accumulation fully intact, so very large fortunes built up under existing rules stay sheltered below that line [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow fairness measure, not a money raiser: it touches only households with $10 million-plus retirement balances, and because so much of the required drawdown can come out of Roth accounts tax-free, the added revenue is small. Its value is mostly in closing the most extreme use of retirement tax shelters; an honest supporter would concede it barely dents the deficit and even leaves a carve-out for closely held business owners.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which has not held a markup or scheduled it for a vote, so it sits with no cosponsors and no action for the rest of this session.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Neal, a senior Democrat on tax policy, introduced the bill on July 21, 2026.
The same day it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which controls tax legislation.
No member joined as a cosponsor, and the committee has taken no further action since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with more than $10 million in retirement accounts are better off, because the bill never advanced and their accounts remain free to keep growing without new limits.

for.name: Rep. Richard E. Neal
for.role: House Ways and Means Committee member and lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Ways and Means Committee.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 21, 2026 and has not scheduled a markup or floor action since.

sides.party_line_note: The only sponsor is a Democrat, no one else signed on, and no votes occurred, so no party split shows up in the record.

industries.note: The bill would stop their further tax-favored contributions and force annual drawdowns of half the excess over $10 million. Their gain under current law — decades of tax-free compounding on outsized balances — is what the bill targets.

industries.industry: Owners of closely held businesses with ESOP accounts
industries.note: The bill exempts ESOP shares not readily tradable on an established market from the accelerated drawdown, keeping a shelter open for this group while closing it for others.
Forced drawdowns would shrink a small slice of mega-account assets under management, but the tax complexity of the new rules creates planning work for the same clients.

analysis.trajectory: With about five months left in this Congress, zero cosponsors, and no committee action since the July 2026 referral, the bill is very unlikely to get a markup or a floor vote before the session ends in January 2027.
